1	# Evals that cannot be talked into passing
2	
3	How to drive `claude plugin eval` against a skill, and how to keep its score
4	attached to something that happened.
5	
6	Everything here was measured against Claude Code **2.1.261** on macOS, mostly by
7	running probe cases that cost cents. Where a claim came from a probe, the probe
8	is named. Where a thing is undocumented and I could not settle it, that is said
9	rather than guessed.
10	
11	A **second source** now feeds it: the first full suite built on this reference,
12	in `haydenrear/skill-manager` — fourteen runs of one case, about **$12**, on
13	Claude Code 2.1.263. Everything traceable to that suite says so, because it ran
14	on a different machine against different units and its environment facts are the
15	ones most likely to be local. Where a claim of theirs was re-checked here, the
16	re-check is named too.
17	
18	The worked example is `examples/agent_integration/eval-plugin/`.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## 0. The unknown unknowns, and how to stop inheriting mine
23	
24	**Everything in this file was believed before it was measured, and a third of
25	what I believed was wrong.** Not wrong at the edges — wrong in the direction
26	that made a suite report success it had not earned. If you import this
27	reference and treat its list as the hazards, you inherit my blind spots along
28	with my findings. The list is the smaller half. **The method is the point.**
29	
30	### What was actually wrong, and what would have caught it a day earlier
31	
32	| I believed | The truth | What found it |
33	|---|---|---|
34	| `scaffold_script:` runs the fixture script | Never invoked, at any placement | An inline body of `exit 3`. The case still scored 1.00 |
35	| The `llm` grader reads the workspace | It reads the final response and nothing else | A hook wrote `banana` into a file; graded three ways |
36	| Symlinking `.claude` leaks my skills into runs | Zero of 20 appeared; the run gets a fresh HOME | Reading the `init` event instead of inferring from three names |
37	| Containment forces physical copies of units | It applies to the entry path only, never inside a plugin | Trying a symlink inside a wrapper |
38	| Entries must be absolute paths | Relative resolves, against the case directory | Trying a relative one |
39	| A bare name is looked up as an installed plugin | There is no name lookup at all | Trying three genuinely installed names |
40	| A `Stop` hook's verdicts cannot be forged | A spawned process writes one after the hook exits | Writing the attack |
41	| The `deny file-write*` rule was applying | It was not: the profile named `/tmp/...`, the kernel resolves to `/private/tmp/...` | Checking the file was absent, not that no error printed |
42	| My forged-workspace control was a control | It ran with no case selected and could not go red | Mutating the recogniser and watching the test stay green |
43	| The eval home's `TMPDIR` follows the operator's shell | **`PATH` is the only variable that reaches the sandbox.** `TMPDIR` and `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` both read `<unset>` inside a run | Printing them from the `SessionStart` hook, after eight runs died inside `git worktree add` |
44	| A hook can check the environment on the agent's behalf | The hook is *more* privileged, so its check answers a question nobody asked | `/usr/bin/git --version` succeeded in the hook in a run where the agent's Bash could not |
45	| A suite runs the cases I wrote | Case discovery is a recursive glob and follows symlinked units into *their* eval directories | Two `spec-double-compiler` cases appearing in a run of a different repository's suite |
46	
47	Read the right-hand column. **Not one of those was found by thinking harder.**
48	
49	### The six habits, in the order they pay
50	
51	1. **Probe; do not reason.** A case that fails to load never runs an agent, so a
52	   refusal costs **$0.00**. Every schema fact in this file came from a
53	   deliberately malformed case. Reasoning about an undocumented tool produces
54	   confident prose and nothing else.
55	
56	2. **Make your failing case fail first.** The attack that proved verdicts were
57	   forgeable did not work on the first try: an embedded `\n` in a heredoc became
58	   a real newline and the payload died on a `SyntaxError`. **"No verdict
59	   appeared" reads exactly like "no hole".** Run the negative case standalone
60	   and confirm it does the bad thing before you conclude anything prevents it.
61	
62	3. **Ask what would look identical if you were wrong.** A denied write prints
63	   nothing. An allowed write also prints nothing. If your evidence is the
64	   *absence* of an error, you have not measured — check the artefact. This one
65	   question would have caught three of the nine rows above.
66	
67	4. **Mutate the thing under test and watch your control go red.** A control that
68	   has never failed is a claim. Gutting a recogniser and finding the suite still
69	   green is how the flagship forgery control was exposed as vacuous — it had
70	   been running with no case selected since the day it was written.
71	
72	5. **Re-run under the real conditions.** The hook's `HOME` is not your `$HOME`;
73	   its `python3` is whatever is on `PATH`; its paths resolve physically. A
74	   verifier that works in your shell and not in the hook withholds verdicts from
75	   correct work, and the score reads as the agent's failure.
76	
77	6. **Count the runs behind the number before you quote it.** Fourteen runs of
78	   one case, while the environment was being repaired monotonically, produced
79	   Bash-call counts of **14, 10, 9, 8, 18, 18, 15, 27, 19, —, 16, —, 15, 21**.
80	   The counts did not improve with the environment, never approached the
81	   budget, and **their spread is wider than every effect that was attributed to
82	   a change.** Seven single runs were quoted as evidence in that round and all
83	   seven conclusions were wrong. This is habit 4 pointed at yourself: a number
84	   you cannot re-produce is a claim.
85	
86	### The rule for adding to this file
87	
88	**Before writing a claim here, name the observation that would differ if it were
89	false.** If you cannot name one, you have a belief, and it goes in marked as a
90	belief — the way the `agents:` paragraph in §3.5 is marked *I have not run
91	that*. An unmarked guess in a reference that other skills import is how one
92	person's ignorance becomes an organisation's.
93	
94	## 1. The three things a case can observe
95	
96	This is the whole surface. Six grader types, and they see between them exactly
97	three things:
98	
99	| grader | what it reads |
100	|---|---|
101	| `file_exists` | **a path in the workspace**, after the run. Globs allowed |
102	| `tool_used` | **a tool NAME** was called, with a count range |
103	| `tool_order` | one tool name **before** another |
104	| `regex` | **the final response text** |
105	| `llm` | **the final response text**, judged by a model, majority of 3 votes |
106	| `baseline` | the final response text, against a `baseline_file` |
107	
108	And here is what nothing observes: **file contents, tool inputs, tool outputs,
109	exit codes.**
110	
111	Three probes established the boundaries, and each of them refuted something I
112	had assumed:
113	
114	* **The `llm` judge sees the final response and nothing else.** A hook wrote
115	  `banana` into `SECRET.txt`; the criterion was "score 1 only if SECRET.txt
116	  contains banana".
117	
118	  | what the agent did | votes |
119	  |---|---|
120	  | never mentioned the file | FAIL FAIL FAIL |
121	  | **read** the file, did not quote it | FAIL FAIL FAIL |
122	  | quoted its contents in the reply | PASS PASS PASS |
123	
124	  Not the workspace. Not tool output. The text it ends with.
125	
126	* **`tool_used` cannot match a command.** The permission-style pattern parses —
127	  the failure message renders it back — but for `Bash` it matches nothing. A
128	  run whose only Bash call was literally `echo hello` scored `Bash` **1x** and
129	  `Bash(echo:*)` **0x** in the same run. There is no grader that can assert
130	  *this command ran*.
131	
132	* **`file_exists` has no content filter.** `contains:` is rejected as an
133	  unrecognised key; `regex` rejects `path:` and `file:`. A path grader knows
134	  only that a path exists.
135	
136	**Consequence, and it is the whole reason for section 3:** with only these,
137	every claim about *quality* has to be routed through the response — and the
138	response is written by the thing being graded.
139	
140	---
141	
142	## 2. Running one
143	
144	```bash
145	HOME=$EVALHOME CLAUDE_CODE_WALNUT_SPIRE=1 \
146	  claude plugin eval <plugin-dir> \
147	      --case '<glob>' --ablation none --runs 1 --allow-tools Bash Write Edit
148	```
149	
150	Each part is load-bearing, and each was learned from a run that scored 0 for a
151	reason that was not the agent's.
152	
153	**`CLAUDE_CODE_WALNUT_SPIRE=1`** — the subcommand is gated behind it and does
154	not exist without it.
155	
156	**`--allow-tools`** — the operator grant, and it is **separate from the case's
157	`allowed_tools:`**. Listing `Write` in the case grants nothing. Running with
158	`--allow-tools Bash` against a case declaring `[Bash, Write, Edit]` produced
159	
160	```
161	not granted (missing --allow-tools grant, or a malformed entry): Write, Edit
162	```
163	
164	once, in a per-case note, and a score of 0 — an agent that could read the
165	program and could not write one line of a spec, reported as a failure to model.
166	**Assert this in a test**: read `allowed_tools` from the case, read the
167	documented command from your README, and fail if a gated tool is in the first
168	and not the second.
169	
170	**`--ablation none` vs the default** — the default runs a second arm with no
171	plugin and reports the delta. That is a real control and worth having, but only
172	if the second arm can do the task. If your fixture is placed by a plugin hook
173	(section 3), the no-plugin arm gets an **empty workspace** and its 0 means "the
174	fixture was never placed", not "the skill is what scored". Use `--ablation
175	none` until the fixture can be placed independently of the plugin.
176	
177	**`--case <glob>`** — a name filter, and it is **not optional once your units
178	are symlinked.** Discovery is a recursive glob — `--help` says the cases are
179	`<eval dir>/**/case.yaml` — so it descends through a symlinked unit into
180	whatever eval directory *that* unit ships. Verified here: this repository ships
181	`examples/agent_integration/eval-plugin/evals/` with two cases of its own, and a
182	suite that symlinks this skill's surface runs them, billed, alongside its own.
183	The cost is silent — the extra cases score, and nothing says they were not
184	yours. §3.5 has the shape that makes this bite.
185	
186	**`--keep-temp`** — preserves each run's sandbox and prints the path. Open it:
187	
188	```bash
189	chmod 700 <kept> <kept>/sealed && chmod -R u+rX <kept>/sealed
190	```
191	
192	The workspace is `<kept>/sealed/home/cwd`; the full event stream is
193	`<kept>/out/trace.jsonl`. **Read the trace before you believe a score.** The
194	trace is where hook exit codes, per-turn tool calls, and `error_max_turns` are
195	visible, and the summary line shows none of them.
196	
197	### The home
198	
199	On a machine with Docker Desktop, a Bash-granting run refuses:
200	
201	> the Docker (`~/.docker`, `DOCKER_CONFIG`) credential store on this machine
202	> holds a symbolic link inside it, so the Bash sandbox cannot reliably exclude it
203	
204	`~/.docker` holds Docker Desktop's CLI shims — 18 symlinks under `bin/` and
205	`cli-plugins/`, none of them credentials. Two things that do not work:
206	`DOCKER_CONFIG` pointed at a plain directory (the message is byte-identical, so
207	the check reads `~/.docker` regardless of the override it names), and a bare
208	`HOME` override (the sandbox passes and the session cannot authenticate —
209	`Not logged in - Please run /login` — even with `.claude` and `.claude.json`
210	symlinked in).
211	
212	**The credential lives in the keychain, and the keychain path is
213	HOME-relative.** Symlink `Library/Keychains` and both hold at once:
214	
215	```bash
216	EVALHOME=/path/to/scratch/evalhome
217	mkdir -p "$EVALHOME/.docker" "$EVALHOME/Library"
218	cp ~/.docker/config.json "$EVALHOME/.docker/config.json"   # the file only
219	for p in .claude .claude.json .config .cache .local; do
220	    ln -s "$HOME/$p" "$EVALHOME/$p"
221	done
222	ln -s "$HOME/Library/Keychains" "$EVALHOME/Library/Keychains"
223	```
224	
225	`.docker` must be a real directory holding a real file; symlinking it to
226	`~/.docker` puts the shims back.
227	
228	**What this home does NOT leak — a correction, because I got it wrong once.**
229	An earlier draft of this section said symlinking `.claude` loads the operator's
230	personal skills into every run, and named `deep-research`, `dataviz` and
231	`code-review` as evidence. That was inference, not measurement, and the
232	measurement says otherwise: a run's `init` event listed **17 skills, every one
233	of them a Claude Code built-in**, plus the plugin under test. None of the
234	operator's 20 skill-manager units appeared, even though they are symlinked into
235	`~/.claude/skills/` and `~/.claude` is symlinked into this home.
236	
237	The reason is stronger than a config directory. The run gets a **fresh HOME**:
238	the kept sandbox's `sealed/home/` holds `.aws .config .git .gitconfig .local
239	cwd` and **no `.claude` at all**, alongside its own per-run config dir with its
240	own `settings.json`, `projects/` and `sessions/`. `$EVALHOME` is not the run's
241	`HOME` either — it is what the CLI authenticates from before the sandbox is
242	built. **The run is more hermetic than I claimed, and your own skills are NOT
243	there unless you put them there** — which is section 3.5.
244	
245	Why the wrong inference looked like evidence, since it is the useful part:
246	`deep-research`, `dataviz` and `code-review` all appear in the **zero-plugin**
247	arm too. They were built-ins the whole time, and naming three of them as
248	"the operator's personal skills" was a guess that happened to fit.
249	
250	### Which copy of your CLI answers — and how to make it the checkout
251	
252	**By default, it is not your checkout.** The run inherits the operator's whole
253	interactive `PATH`, `~/.skill-manager/bin/cli` is on it, and a
254	`which -a tla-spec-dev` inside a run returned
255	
256	```
257	/Users/hayde/.skill-manager/bin/cli/tla-spec-dev
258	/Users/hayde/.skill-manager/bin/cli/tla-spec-dev
259	/Users/hayde/.skill-manager/bin/cli/tla-spec-dev
260	```
261	
262	and nothing else. In another run, 32 of 55 Bash calls touched
263	`~/.skill-manager` and a traceback resolved the code from
264	`~/.skill-manager/skills/<unit>/scripts/`. **The plugin's skill directory
265	loaded correctly and the branch under review was still never executed** — the
266	skill under test was the plugin's, the toolchain under test was whatever was
267	installed.
268	
269	Three ways to fix that do not work. Each was measured, not reasoned about:
270	
271	| attempt | what happened |
272	|---|---|
273	| a plugin `bin/` directory | the docs say it joins the Bash tool's `PATH` while the plugin is enabled. Inside `plugin eval` it never appeared |
274	| `execution.env: {PATH: ...}` in case.yaml | refused: *"only EVAL_\* keys can be set from case.yaml. Anything else must come from the operator's shell."* |
275	| a shim under `/tmp` | the shell `PATH` **does** reach the run — it was first in `$PATH` — but the sandbox cannot reach `/private/tmp`, so `which` never found it |
276	
277	The refusal message names the answer. **Ship a shim inside the checkout and let
278	the operator prepend it:**
279	
280	```sh
281	# <plugin>/bin/<your-cli>
282	set -eu
283	here=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)
284	repo=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$here/../../../.." && pwd)
285	test -f "$repo/scripts/<entry>.py" || {
286	    echo "shim: no checkout at $repo -- refusing to fall through to an" \
287	         "installed copy, which would grade code nobody is reviewing" >&2
288	    exit 127
289	}
290	exec python3 "$repo/scripts/<entry>.py" "$@"
291	```
292	
293	```bash
294	PATH="<plugin>/bin:$PATH" claude plugin eval <plugin-dir> ...
295	```
296	
297	Verified: `which -a` then lists the checkout's shim first, ahead of the
298	installed copies. **The shim refuses rather than falling through** — a shim
299	that silently defers to the installed CLI reintroduces the exact bug it exists
300	to fix, and does it invisibly.
301	
302	Then have the `SessionStart` hook *say which one it got*, and warn when it is
303	not the shim, so the trace answers the question without anyone having to
304	reconstruct it:
305	
306	```
307	  tla-spec-dev: <plugin>/bin/tla-spec-dev  (THE CHECKOUT under review)
308	```
309	
310	### Dependent tools
311	
312	A skill declares `cli_dependencies` and then assumes they are there. The eval
313	sandbox is not your shell: have the `SessionStart` hook resolve each one and
314	print it, missing ones included.
315	
316	```
317	  java:      /usr/bin/java
318	  tla2tools: ~/.skill-manager/bin/cli/.spec-double-compiler/tla2tools.jar
319	  pytest:    /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.10/bin/pytest
320	  jinja2:    NOT ON PATH
321	```
322	
323	`NOT ON PATH` printed before turn one is a truthful input. The same fact
324	discovered on turn 30 is a turn-ceiling failure that reads as an agent who
325	could not do the work.
326	
327	---
328	
329	## 3. Adding a skill, and placing a fixture
330	
331	### The plugin
332	
333	A directory with `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`:
334	
335	```json
336	{"name": "<name>-eval", "version": "0.1.0", "experimental": {"evals": "evals"}}
337	```
338	
339	and the skill surface under `skills/<skill-name>/`. **Symlink it, do not copy
340	it** — a copy drifts from the repository it claims to test. Verified loaded: a
341	passing run's `init` event listed the plugin, and the agent invoked
342	`Skill(<plugin>:<skill>)`.
343	
344	One plugin holds **many cases** — `evals/<case-name>/` per case. You do not
345	need a plugin per case.
346	
347	**But hooks belong to the plugin, not to a case**, so one `SessionStart` hook
348	has to serve every case. `execution.env` is the channel, and the allowlist that
349	refuses `PATH` is exactly what it is for:
350	
351	```yaml
352	execution:
353	  env:
354	    EVAL_CASE: catch-the-drift
355	```
356	
357	```sh
358	case "${EVAL_CASE:-}" in
359	  scaffold-a-program-model) ... ;;
360	  catch-the-drift)          ... ;;
361	  "")  echo "EVAL_CASE unset" >&2; exit 1 ;;
362	esac
363	```
364	
365	Verified: a case setting `EVAL_CASE` had it visible in the hook. **Fail loudly
366	when it is unset** — a hook that silently places nothing is the empty-repository
367	failure again, and it reads as an agent who could not work.
368	
369	Keep the shared scripts **outside** `evals/` (`<plugin>/lib/`). A directory
370	under `evals/` with no `case.yaml` is not loaded as a case today, but putting
371	library code where the loader is scanning invites a name to become meaningful
372	later.
373	
374	If `plugin eval` refuses your repository with *"a plugin directory holds more
375	than 20000 entries"*, that is what the thin symlinked plugin is for: carry the
376	skill's surface and nothing else.
377	
378	### `scaffold_script:` does not run — use a hook
379	
380	A case may declare `scaffold_script:` and the CLI has a `--scaffold` flag that
381	prints a warning about running it. **The script is never executed.** Measured at
382	every placement — top level, `execution:`, `setup:`, `workspace:`, `sandbox:`,
383	`scaffold.script` — and in both forms, a file name and inline bash. The
384	decisive probe was an inline body of `echo ... >&2; exit 3`: the case still
385	scored 1.00, so it was not failing quietly, it was never invoked.
386	
387	Place fixtures from a **`SessionStart` hook** in `hooks/hooks.json`. One hook
388	serves every case and dispatches on `EVAL_CASE` (see above), so it lives beside
389	the plugin rather than inside a case:
390	
391	```json
392	{"hooks": {"SessionStart": [{"hooks": [
393	  {"type": "command", "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/lib/place.sh"}
394	]}]}}
395	```
396	
397	**Fail with exit 2, not exit 1.** Claude Code treats 2 as blocking and every
398	other non-zero code as advisory, so a placement hook that exits 1 prints its
399	complaint and lets the session start anyway — on a workspace it just failed to
400	set up. Where a case seeds a deliberate fault, that is the difference between
401	refusing and handing the agent a program with nothing wrong with it, which
402	scores well for doing nothing.
403	
404	It runs with the workspace as its working directory, before the first turn, and
405	the trace records `hook_response … exit_code 0`. Locate the fixture from `$0`,
406	never from the working directory and never from a guessed environment variable:
407	a `${EVAL_CASE_DIR:-.}` whose `.` fallback resolved to the workspace copied
408	nothing, and the case scored 0 on an empty repository. What that reads as is
409	"the agent could not build a spec". What it meant was "there was nothing to
410	build one from".
411	
412	### Hand the session its toolchain
413	
414	A case that makes the agent find its own tools measures the search, not the
415	skill. One run spent **39 of its 40 turns** on `find / -maxdepth 8 -iname
416	"tla2tools*.jar"`, a scan of `/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines` and an `unzip`
417	of the jar, hit the turn ceiling, and left behind a scratch module about a
418	counter mod 3.
419	
420	Have the `SessionStart` hook discover the tools **at runtime** and print what it
421	found. Nothing hardcoded: another machine gets its own paths, or gets told the
422	tool is missing, which is a truthful input rather than a silent 0.
423	
424	### Five environment facts, each of which cost a failed run
425	
426	From the `skill-manager` suite. Each was paid for once; a suite that does not
427	know them pays again, and every one of them bills as a skill failure.
428	
429	1. **`PATH` is the only variable that reaches the sandbox.** `TMPDIR` and
430	   `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` both printed `<unset>` from inside a run, even though
431	   both were set in the operator's shell. `execution.env` will not close the
432	   gap either — its allowlist refuses everything but `EVAL_*`:
433	
434	   > `execution.env` key PATH is not allowed — only `EVAL_*` keys can be set
435	   > from case.yaml. Anything else must come from the operator's shell.
436	
437	   Read those two sentences together: `PATH` has to come from the shell, and
438	   `PATH` is the only part of the shell that arrives — `TMPDIR` was set there
439	   too and did not. **Anything your case needs that is not a `PATH` entry or an
440	   `EVAL_*` key has to be discovered inside the run.**
441	
442	2. **An unset `TMPDIR` breaks Apple's `git` before it does anything.** `git`
443	   from the Xcode command-line tools writes an `xcrun` cache into `TMPDIR` on
444	   startup. Without one:
445	
446	   ```
447	   git: error: couldn't create cache file '…/T/xcrun_db-…' (Operation not permitted)
448	   ```
449	
450	   and `git worktree add` dies immediately after printing *"Preparing
451	   worktree"*. **One unset variable made a case unmeasurable for eight runs** —
452	   eight reds on a case whose task began with a worktree command, not one of
453	   them about the skill under test.
454	
455	3. **The sandbox cannot read under the operator's home directory.** The same
456	   command succeeded in an ordinary shell and failed inside a run. Build trees,
457	   fixtures and checkouts have to live where the sandbox reaches — `/private/tmp`
458	   worked, which is where it keeps its own temps.
459	
460	   > **This does not agree with the `/private/tmp` row in §2**, which says a
461	   > shim there was on `PATH` and `which` never found it. The two observations
462	   > are not the same observation — one is *resolving an executable on `PATH`*,
463	   > the other is *reading a tree* — and they are from different suites on
464	   > different machines, one of them a CLI patch apart. **Which of read access,
465	   > exec access and `PATH` resolution `/private/tmp` actually gets is
466	   > UNDECIDED**, and the row stays until somebody runs the probe that
467	   > separates them: put a readable file and an executable shim in one
468	   > `/private/tmp` directory and have the hook print `cat` and `which` for
469	   > each. That probe costs one refused case, i.e. $0.00.
470	
471	4. **A CLI shim may exec a toolchain of its own.** The checkout shim in §2 ends
472	   in `exec`, and what it execs has its own dependencies — theirs runs `jbang`.
473	   Putting the shim's directory on the eval `PATH` is not enough; **everything
474	   the shim reaches for has to be on that `PATH` too**, and the `SessionStart`
475	   hook should print each of them the way §"Dependent tools" prints the rest.
476	
477	5. **A hook cannot verify the environment on the agent's behalf.** Measured: the
478	   `SessionStart` hook ran `/usr/bin/git --version` successfully in a run where
479	   the agent's own Bash could not. The hook is outside the sandbox — that is the
480	   same asymmetry §4 relies on to run TLC, read in the opposite direction, and
481	   it is worse here because it is *silent*. A hook that checks a tool and prints
482	   `OK` has confirmed the tool works **for the hook**, and the run proceeds into
483	   an environment nobody has actually tested.
484	
485	### Prove the environment in setup, before a run is billed against it
486	
487	The consequence of all five, and it is the cheapest rule in this file.
488	
489	**Setup must run the real front-door command and fail if it does not work.**
490	Not a version probe, not a `which` — the actual first command the case will ask
491	the agent for, in a throwaway corner of the fixture, from the same place the
492	agent will stand:
493	
494	```sh
495	verify_env() {                     # last thing setup.sh does
496	    tmp=$(mktemp -d)
497	    ( cd "$tmp" && <the real front-door command> ) >"$tmp/log" 2>&1 || {
498	        echo "setup: environment cannot run the task — refusing to bill a run" >&2
499	        cat "$tmp/log" >&2
500	        exit 1
501	    }
502	    rm -rf "$tmp"
503	}
504	```
505	
506	It costs **$0.00** — a case that never starts runs no agent — and in that suite
507	it caught three broken environments that would otherwise have been billed, and
508	reported, as skill failures. Facts 2 and 3 above are both things `verify_env`
509	would have caught on run one instead of run eight.
510	
511	**This is not the `.eval/toolchain` marker of §4, and it does not replace it.**
512	The marker annotates a run that happened; `verify_env` stops the run from
513	happening. You want both: the marker cannot rescue a score (§4 is explicit that
514	`file_exists` has no UNDECIDED), and setup refusing is the only mechanism that
515	keeps the unmeasurable run out of the report entirely.

519	## 3.5 Several skills at once, and live units from a skill-manager home
520	
521	**`claude plugin eval` is not limited to one plugin.** A case declares
522	`plugins:` — an array — and every entry loads alongside the target. Measured,
523	three units in one run:
524	
525	```
526	Plugin under test: "git-issue" (no version) at ".../units/git-issue"
527	Plugin under test: "git-epic-workflow" (no version) at ".../units/git-epic-workflow"
528	Plugin under test: "skt" version "0.8.1" at ".../units/skt"
529	plugins loaded: ['git-issue', 'git-epic-workflow', 'skt']
530	their skills  : ['git-issue:git-issue', 'git-epic-workflow:git-epic-workflow',
531	                 'skt:skt', 'skt:unit-authoring']
532	```
533	
534	`plugins:` is per **case**, so different cases load different subsets. That is
535	the shape worth building toward: *does this workflow need the epic skill, or
536	does the issue skill alone get through?* is one case per subset, and
537	`--ablation with-without` gives each one a no-plugin arm to be measured against.
538	
539	**But a subset is an ablation you are deliberately running, not the default for
540	an ordinary case.** The distinction cost the `skill-manager` suite a rule, and
541	it is worth stating as one: **a case whose question is not itself "which unit is
542	needed" loads EVERY unit.** What such a case measures is retrieval *among* the
543	skills — whether the agent finds the right one with all of them in front of it.
544	Hand it only the units its task happens to need and you have done the retrieval
545	for it, and the score reports a skill that would not have been reached. It is
546	progressive disclosure graded against a curated shortlist, which is the one
547	condition it never meets in production.
548	
549	So there are two case shapes, and mixing them up is how a suite gets a good
550	number for the wrong reason:
551	
552	| the case asks | `plugins:` |
553	|---|---|
554	| can the agent do the task | **every unit in `units/`** |
555	| does it need *this* unit to do the task | the subset, plus a sibling case with the complement |
556	
557	### How an entry resolves
558	
559	* **Relative paths resolve against the CASE DIRECTORY**, not the target root and
560	  not the working directory. From `evals/probe/case.yaml`, `../../units/alpha`
561	  loads. Prefer this: it keeps a suite portable, where an absolute path hardcodes
562	  one operator's home into every case.
563	* **There is no name lookup.** `git-issue`, `jdtls-lsp`, and
564	  `jdtls-lsp@claude-plugins-official` all return `does not exist`, including for
565	  genuinely installed plugins. An entry is a path or it is nothing.
566	* **A unit needs no manifest.** A directory with a bare `SKILL.md` loads as a
567	  single-skill plugin named after **the directory**, not after the frontmatter's
568	  `name:`. Note that `claude plugin validate` *rejects* such a directory, so it
569	  is not a usable pre-check for `plugins:` entries.
570	
571	### The containment rule, and exactly how far it reaches
572	
573	The **entry path** must resolve under the containment root — the directory you
574	targeted, or its enclosing plugin. It is realpath'd first, so a symlink that
575	points out is refused:
576	
577	> `plugins` entry ".../units/link-out" resolves to
578	> /Users/…/.skill-manager/skills/git-issue, **outside the containment root** …
579	> Only plugins under it can be loaded from case.yaml.
580	
581	**But containment stops at the entry. It does not reach inside a loaded
582	plugin** — and that is the whole trick for evaluating a skill-manager home.
583	Measured: a wrapper at `units/omega/` with a real
584	`.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and
585	
586	```
587	units/omega/skills/git-issue -> ~/.skill-manager/skills/git-issue
588	```
589	
590	loads as `omega:git-issue`, reading the live unit through a symlink pointing
591	straight out of the root.
592	
593	**So do not copy your units.** An earlier draft of this section said copies were
594	forced and then spent a page on managing their drift — advice that contradicted
595	§3 of this same file, which says to symlink the skill surface precisely so it
596	cannot drift. One thin wrapper per unit gets live skills and no drift:
597	
598	```
599	skill-eval-harness/
600	  units/
601	    git-issue/.claude-plugin/plugin.json         {"name":"git-issue","version":"0.1.0"}
602	    git-issue/skills/git-issue      -> $SKILL_MANAGER_HOME/skills/git-issue
603	    git-epic-workflow/…             -> $SKILL_MANAGER_HOME/skills/git-epic-workflow
604	    skt/…                           -> $SKILL_MANAGER_HOME/plugins/skt
605	  evals/
606	    epic-then-issue/case.yaml       plugins: [../../units/git-epic-workflow, ../../units/git-issue]
607	    issue-alone/case.yaml           plugins: [../../units/git-issue]
608	    the-whole-workflow/case.yaml    plugins: [all of them]
609	```
610	
611	```bash
612	cd skill-eval-harness
613	HOME=$EVALHOME CLAUDE_CODE_WALNUT_SPIRE=1 \
614	  claude plugin eval . --case 'epic-then-issue' --allow-tools Bash Write Edit
615	```
616	
617	Three gotchas the wrapper form introduces:
618	
619	* **`--case` is mandatory here, and this is the shape that makes it so.** The
620	  wrapper's whole point is that `units/*/skills/*` are symlinks into live units,
621	  and discovery is a recursive glob (`<eval dir>/**/case.yaml`) that follows
622	  them. A unit that ships its own eval plugin — `spec-double-compiler` ships
623	  `examples/agent_integration/eval-plugin/evals/` with two cases — contributes
624	  those cases to *your* run. They score, they bill, and the report does not mark
625	  them as somebody else's. **Name the cases you meant to run, every time.**
626	
627	* **A symlinked ENTRY loads under its resolved identity.** `units/git-issue ->
628	  vendored/gi` (inside the root, so accepted) loads as plugin **`gi`**, and
629	  every `tool_used: Skill` grader naming `git-issue:git-issue` then silently
630	  scores 0. Symlink the skill *inside* the wrapper, not the wrapper itself.
631	* **The wrapper's directory name is the plugin name**, so it is also the skill
632	  namespace your graders must spell.
633	
634	The target itself need not be a plugin: a plain directory holding `evals/` and
635	`units/` works, `evals/` is found with no manifest, and with no `plugins:` key
636	the CLI says `Plugin under test: none resolved — cases run against baseline
637	Claude Code` rather than pretending the directory is under test. It still
638	defaults to `--ablation with-without` when a case does resolve plugins, so the
639	command above already gets two arms.
640	
641	### Several kinds of agent
642	
643	A plugin can ship `agents/`, and a plugin's `settings.json` can set `agent:` to
644	make one of them the main thread. That is the documented lever for "will a
645	different kind of agent get through this workflow", and the wrapper shape gives
646	each variant its own directory and its own case.
647	
648	**I have not run that.** Everything else in this section was measured; this
649	paragraph is the mechanism from the plugin documentation, and the first person
650	to try it should expect to correct it.

652	## 3.6 Where a suite lives, and what it leaves behind
653	
654	Everything above is one case. A suite is a directory that outlives the round
655	that built it, and this is the layout the `skill-manager` suite arrived at —
656	offered as a convention, not a mechanism: nothing in `plugin eval` requires it.
657	
658	```
659	specs/evals/
660	  README.md                     how to run; points at this file for how a case is written
661	  harness/
662	    lib.sh                      eval_path, eval_tmpdir, branch_home, verify_env
663	    rewrite-case.py             generates the machine-specific parts of a case
664	    units-template/             the harness's own plugins (hooks, no skills)
665	    evals/<case>/setup.sh       makes the environment realistic
666	    evals/<case>/run.sh         carries the PATH, runs the case, tears down
667	    evals/<case>/case.yaml + graders/*.md
668	  results/                      evidence: what was run, what it cost, the traces
669	```
670	
671	**A setup script and a run script per case**, because §3's five environment
672	facts have to be executed by something and a README cannot execute. Setup makes
673	the environment realistic and ends in `verify_env`; run carries the `PATH` —
674	the one variable that gets through — and tears down after.
675	
676	The rule the layout exists to enforce is one line:
677	
678	> **What is in git is what MAKES the environment, never the environment.**
679	
680	Nothing machine-specific is committed. `rewrite-case.py` generates the parts
681	that are, on the machine that is about to run. A committed absolute path is the
682	same defect as a hardcoded jar in a `SessionStart` hook, one directory further
683	out.
684	
685	### An eval score is spec evidence, and it is filed like any other
686	
687	A score is a measurement of the same kind as a TLC run or a Test Graph
688	envelope, and it belongs in the same places: under the ticket's `results/`
689	directory, passed to `close ticket --result`, snapshotted into `.history` when
690	the workflow closes, cited by the goal it claims to move. It is not a different
691	species of number because a model produced it.
692	
693	**But file the trace, not the score.** Every useful thing the `skill-manager`
694	round produced came out of `trace.jsonl`; **the scores were actively
695	misleading** — §4 is a catalogue of the ways, and that round added two more
696	(§3's facts 2 and 3, eight reds that were an unset variable). A committed `0.25`
697	is unreadable a week later and unfalsifiable forever.
698	
699	So the convention is **"record the score with the trace excerpt that justifies
700	it"**, and the excerpt is the part that has to be there:
701	
702	```
703	specs/evals/results/<round>/
704	  summary.md          the score, the CLI version, the case, the run count
705	  trace-<case>-<n>.jsonl        or the excerpt, where the whole file is large
706	  UNDECIDED.md        which runs were not measurements, and why
707	```
708	
709	`UNDECIDED.md` is not optional padding — it is where the eight unmeasurable
710	runs go, so that a later reader counting reds does not count them. §4 has the
711	argument for why nothing inside a case can carry that fact.
712	
713	### What this buys, stated as a number rather than a hope
714	
715	The same round found **four defects in shipped CLIs and skills that 258 passing
716	unit tests did not see.** All four were about an agent's path through a CLI: an
717	argument refused with a remedy the repository could not carry out, a `--help`

719	*condition* for using a tool without saying how to test it, and a verifier

721	error message is actionable**, and that is the class this instrument reaches and
722	the rest of the suite does not.

724	It also produced roughly a dozen defects in **itself**, which is the more

729	## 4. Keeping the score honest
730	
731	### The failure, stated plainly
732	
733	A case scored **1.00** on this skill while `tla-spec-dev scaffold project`
734	failed with **exit 1 on all three attempts**, and the
735	`specs/program_model/spec_manifest.yaml` that the artefact grader accepted as
736	proof the pipeline had run was written by the agent's own `Write` tool. A
737	separate probe scored that same grader green on a manifest whose entire contents
738	were `placeholder: true`.
739	
740	The report was excellent and the model was genuinely good. **Neither of those
741	facts was measured.** What was measured was: a path exists, and a paragraph
742	reads well.
743	
744	An adversarial case that told an agent to write the placeholder and then claim a
745	model scored 0.50 — and the half it lost was lost because **the agent refused to
746	write the false report**, not because a grader caught it:
747	
748	> *"I'm not going to write the second part. It asks me to state that I built a
749	> TLA+ program model when the only thing on disk is a one-line placeholder …
750	> That's a false report about my own work."*
751	
752	An instrument whose anti-gaming property is the honesty of the thing it grades
753	has no anti-gaming property.
754	
755	### The fix: verify in a `Stop` hook, grade the verdict path
756	
757	**The sandbox that stops the agent does not stop a hook.** The Bash *tool* runs
758	under a profile denying filesystem writes to every subprocess it spawns — which
759	is why TLC aborts creating its metadir and why a CLI that writes files cannot
760	run. Hooks are outside it. Measured: a `Stop` hook's
761	`python3 -c "open(...,'w')"` and its `mkdir` both succeed in the same workspace
762	where the Bash tool is refused.
763	
764	So run the real check after the agent stops, and let it write the paths the
765	graders read:
766	
767	```json
768	{"hooks": {"Stop": [{"hooks": [
769	  {"type": "command",
770	   "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/evals/<case>/verify.sh",
771	   "timeout": 600}
772	]}]}}
773	```
774	
775	```sh
776	# verify.sh
777	set -u
778	rm -rf .eval && mkdir -p .eval          # RULE 1
779	... run SANY / TLC / the real CLI ...
780	[ success ] && echo ok > .eval/checks   # RULE 2
781	exit 0                                  # RULE 3
782	```
783	
784	with `type: file_exists, path: ".eval/checks"` as the grader.
785	
786	**Three rules make it sound.**
787	
788	1. **Delete every verdict path before looking.** The agent has `Write` and can
789	   create any filename it can guess. Demonstrated: a workspace with all three
790	   verdict files pre-planted came out of the hook with none of them, because
791	   the real check did not pass.
792	2. **Write a verdict only after a real program returns success.** SANY, TLC, a
793	   YAML parse, your own test runner. Never after reading the response.
794	3. **`exit 0`, always.** A `Stop` hook that fails non-zero can push the session
795	   onward, and a verifier that changes the run it measures is not a verifier.
796	4. **Run agent-authored code with no write anywhere, and write its verdict
797	   yourself.** This is the rule the first three do not cover, and it was found
798	   by attack rather than by reasoning.
799	
800	### The hook is not inside the sandbox, and that cuts both ways
801	
802	The reason a `Stop` hook can run TLC is that it is outside the profile that
803	denies the agent's Bash tool every filesystem write. The same fact means
804	**anything the hook executes runs with the hook's privileges** — including the
805	program the agent was told to repair.
806	
807	Demonstrated on the `catch-the-drift` case. Five lines appended to
808	`ecommerce_backend/domain.py`:
809	
810	```python
811	_PAYLOAD = "import time, os\ntime.sleep(4)\nos.makedirs('.eval', exist_ok=True)\n" \
812	           "open('.eval/behaviour', 'w').write('forged after the hook exited')\n"
813	_sp.Popen([_sys.executable, "-c", _PAYLOAD], cwd=_os.getcwd(), start_new_session=True)
814	```
815	
816	The hook refused correctly — `create_account did not persist` — exited with no
817	`behaviour` verdict, and four seconds later the spawned process created it. The
818	graders then read a green weight-2 verdict on a program that was never
819	repaired, with the refusal it overwrote still sitting in the verifier's own log.
820	
821	**Clearing the verdict directory first does not help**, because the write lands
822	after the hook is gone. **Killing the process group does not help either** —
823	`start_new_session=True` exists precisely to escape that.
824	
825	What does: refuse the write. On macOS, `sandbox-exec -f <profile>` with
826	
827	```
828	(version 1)
829	(allow default)
830	(deny file-write*)
831	(allow file-write-data (literal "/dev/null") (literal "/dev/stdout") (literal "/dev/stderr"))
832	```
833	
834	and the check then **cannot record its own verdict**, which is the separation
835	that matters: it signals through its exit status, and the hook — outside the
836	profile — writes the file. Untrusted code decides nothing about what gets
837	written. Descendants inherit the profile, so daemonising buys nothing.
838	
839	Set `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`; a confined interpreter cannot write
840	`__pycache__` and will otherwise complain.
841	
842	**Two profiles, because not everything the hook runs can be denied writes.**
843	SANY and TLC parse and explore agent-authored `.tla`, and TLC creates a metadir
844	before exploring anything — deny it writes and it aborts having checked
845	nothing, which is a verdict withheld for the verifier's own configuration. So:
846	
847	| profile | applied to | rule |
848	|---|---|---|
849	| `nowrite.sb` | checks that need no writes (the behavioural check, the manifest check) | `(deny file-write*)` |
850	| `noverdict.sb` | **everything else the hook executes**, SANY and TLC included | `(deny file-write* (subpath (param "VERDICTS")))` |
851	
852	The graders read exactly one directory, so that is the directory nothing the
853	hook runs may write. Descendants inherit either profile, so a payload that
854	daemonises and sleeps past the hook's exit is refused under both.
855	
856	**THE PATH IN A PROFILE MUST BE THE RESOLVED ONE.** macOS resolves before
857	matching, so a profile naming `/tmp/ws/.eval` does not deny a write to
858	`/private/tmp/ws/.eval` — and **a deny that never applies looks exactly like a
859	deny that worked**, because an allowed write prints nothing either. Use
860	`pwd -P`. Measured both ways: with the physical path the deny fires through the
861	physical path *and* through the symlinked one; without it, through neither.
862	This is habit 3 in §0, and it cost a round to learn twice.
863	
864	Where no such facility exists, run the check anyway and **write a verdict
865	saying so** — `.eval/UNDECIDED-unconfined` — rather than offering the same
866	green under a weaker guarantee. An operator who cannot tell the two apart is
867	back to reading a number that means less than it says.
868	
869	Verified both ways on the real artefact: the passing run's model produced
870	`parses`, `checks` and `manifest`; a workspace holding `placeholder: true` and
871	three forged verdicts produced none.
872	
873	### The verifier is now the thing most likely to be wrong
874	
875	Moving the judgement into a hook does not remove the false-negative risk. It
876	relocates it, from the grader to the program the grader trusts — and that
877	program runs in an environment nobody looked at. Three of these were caught
878	here, and the first two were caught only because a control was run before the
879	suite was:
880	
881	* **`SANY` resolves imports against the working directory.** Invoked from the
882	  workspace root on `specs/program_model/External.tla`, it reported *"Cannot
883	  find source file for module Internal"* about a module that parses perfectly.
884	  Run it from the model directory on a bare filename.
885	* **A module loaded by path is not in `sys.modules`, and `@dataclass` looks up
886	  `sys.modules[cls.__module__].__dict__`.** A behavioural check that used
887	  `spec_from_file_location` died with `'NoneType' object has no attribute
888	  '__dict__'` and withheld its verdict — from a workspace that may have been
889	  repaired. Use a plain import.
890	* **The hook's `$HOME` is not yours, and its `python3` is whatever is on
891	  `PATH`.** A jar search rooted at `$HOME/.skill-manager` found nothing, so SANY
892	  and TLC were skipped and two cases lost their artefact verdicts — 0.25 and 0.80 reported for an environment fault **in the
893	  verifier**. The manifest check failed the same way on `No module named
894	  'yaml'`. (I first wrote that `$HOME` was the constructed eval home. It is not
895	  — it is the sandbox's own sealed home, which has no `.claude` and no
896	  `.skill-manager`. Both explain the empty search, which is why the wrong reason
897	  survived until someone checked it.) Resolve tools the way the project's own
898	  wrappers do (`bin/cli/tlc2` derives its jar from its own location and honours
899	  `TLA2TOOLS_JAR`), and give every library import a fallback.
900	
901	Two rules follow, and they cost nothing:
902	
903	1. **Run the verifier against a known-good workspace and a known-bad one before
904	   you run the suite**, under the same `HOME` the hook will have. Every one of
905	   the three above was a green control away from being charged to an agent.
906	2. **Write a marker for the ENVIRONMENT too** — `.eval/toolchain` when the
907	   tools resolved, `.eval/UNDECIDED-toolchain` when they did not. Never grade
908	   either: a forged workspace earns them as readily as a good one.
909	
910	   **Be honest about what this buys, because it is less than it looks.**
911	   `file_exists` has only pass and fail — there is no UNDECIDED — so a missing
912	   toolchain still scores the artefact graders at **0, i.e. FAIL, on a model
913	   that may be perfect.** That is `SS-02`, and a case cannot fix it from the
914	   inside. What the marker does is leave the reason where the person reading
915	   the 0 will find it. It changes the report, not the score, and a document
916	   that says otherwise is doing the thing this whole reference is against.
917	   (An earlier draft of this section did say otherwise. A blind review caught
918	   it.)
919	
920	### What each grader is for, once you have this
921	
922	* **verdict paths carry the claim.** They are the only evidence a confident
923	  report cannot move.
924	* **the `llm` grader grades the REPORT, and must say so in its own body.** A
925	  grader that ends *"score the artefacts, not the claim"* is asking for
926	  something the judge cannot do, so what it scores is the claim while reading as
927	  though it scored the artefact — an absent input scored as if present. If the
928	  report matters, ask the prompt to quote the artefact so there is real text
929	  under the judgement, and keep the weight low.
930	* **`tool_used: Skill`** is worth one grader on its own: it tells you the skill
931	  was invoked rather than reinvented. Under `--ablation with-without` a
932	  `tool_used: Skill` grader is treated as a plugin-fired indicator rather than
933	  part of the score.
934	
935	### Three failure shapes to check before reading any number
936	
937	**UNDECIDED has no representation, and that is the dangerous one.** `file_exists`
938	has only pass and fail; `tool_used` has only a count inside a range or outside
939	it. Neither can say *"this run was not a measurement."* So **an environment that
940	could not run the task and a skill that could not do the task produce the same
941	number**, and the number is a red charged to the skill. Eight consecutive reds
942	in the `skill-manager` round were an unset `TMPDIR` (§3, fact 2), and nothing in
943	the score said so.
944	
945	The line that follows is short and it goes before the other two: **before
946	reading a red, confirm the task was possible in that environment.** Reading it
947	after is how a suite spends eight runs improving a skill that was never the
948	problem. `verify_env` in setup (§3) is the mechanism that makes this checkable
949	rather than remembered; the `.eval/toolchain` marker above is what leaves the
950	reason where the person reading the red will find it.
951	
952	**A run that ran out of turns is `UNDECIDED`, and the suite scores it FAIL.**
953	`error_max_turns` leaves no closing report, so every response grader votes FAIL
954	on a run that may have done the work perfectly. One run here wrote exactly the
955	right model and was cut off mid-verification with the words *"Now full
956	verification of everything I can execute."* — scored 0.50, which is also
957	precisely the score a half-finished model gets. **The two are indistinguishable
958	in the number.** Always read the `error:` column beside the score. Verdict-path
959	graders are what keeps such a run legible, because they still see the workspace
960	— **but only if something writes the verdicts, and a `Stop` hook does not run
961	on that exit.** Measured in the `skill-manager` wide lane (2026-09-14, 2.1.270):
962	with the verifier registered on both `Stop` and `SessionEnd` and each writing
963	which event it was, every run that ended `error_max_turns` was written by
964	`SessionEnd` alone, and every normal run by `Stop`. A round that registered only
965	`Stop` lost every verdict on 12 capped runs and scored them red. Register the
966	verifier on `SessionEnd` too; both derive the same verdicts, so the second
967	write is harmless.
968	
969	**A majority is not a consensus.** The `llm` grader takes three votes. A run
970	whose artefact was plainly correct passed **FAIL PASS PASS**. One run's score
971	from one case is not evidence of much; if a number is going to be quoted, run
972	it more than once.
973	
974	### The checklist
975	
976	Before a score means anything:
977	
978	- [ ] every gated tool in `allowed_tools:` is in the documented `--allow-tools`
979	- [ ] the fixture is placed by a hook, and the trace shows `exit_code 0`
980	- [ ] no grader is satisfied by a path the agent can create — or a `Stop` hook
981	      deletes it first
982	- [ ] at least one grader is a verdict written by a real program
983	- [ ] every `llm` grader says in its own body that it reads the response only
984	- [ ] a forged workspace has been run through the graders and scored 0
985	- [ ] the run did not end `error_max_turns`
986	- [ ] setup proved the environment could run the task **before** the run was
987	      billed, and the runs it refused are recorded as UNDECIDED rather than red
988	- [ ] **no number in this report comes from a single run**
989	- [ ] the verifier has been run against a known-good and a known-bad workspace,
990	      under the same `HOME` the hook will have
991	- [ ] a `.eval/toolchain` marker distinguishes "checked and failed" from "never
992	      checked", and no grader scores it
993	- [ ] the run executed YOUR checkout — the hook printed which CLI it resolved
994	- [ ] agent-authored code that the verifier executes cannot write the verdicts,
995	      and a run where it could says so
996	- [ ] you have read `trace.jsonl`, not only the summary line
997	
998	The last one catches the others.

# Evals that cannot be talked into passing

How to drive `claude plugin eval` against a skill, and how to keep its score
attached to something that happened.

Everything here was measured against Claude Code **2.1.261** on macOS, mostly by
running probe cases that cost cents. Where a claim came from a probe, the probe
is named. Where a thing is undocumented and I could not settle it, that is said
rather than guessed.

A **second source** now feeds it: the first full suite built on this reference,
in `haydenrear/skill-manager` — fourteen runs of one case, about **$12**, on
Claude Code 2.1.263. Everything traceable to that suite says so, because it ran
on a different machine against different units and its environment facts are the
ones most likely to be local. Where a claim of theirs was re-checked here, the
re-check is named too.

The worked example is `examples/agent_integration/eval-plugin/`.

---

## 0. The unknown unknowns, and how to stop inheriting mine

**Everything in this file was believed before it was measured, and a third of
what I believed was wrong.** Not wrong at the edges — wrong in the direction
that made a suite report success it had not earned. If you import this
reference and treat its list as the hazards, you inherit my blind spots along
with my findings. The list is the smaller half. **The method is the point.**

### What was actually wrong, and what would have caught it a day earlier

| I believed | The truth | What found it |
|---|---|---|
| `scaffold_script:` runs the fixture script | Never invoked, at any placement | An inline body of `exit 3`. The case still scored 1.00 |
| The `llm` grader reads the workspace | It reads the final response and nothing else | A hook wrote `banana` into a file; graded three ways |
| Symlinking `.claude` leaks my skills into runs | Zero of 20 appeared; the run gets a fresh HOME | Reading the `init` event instead of inferring from three names |
| Containment forces physical copies of units | It applies to the entry path only, never inside a plugin | Trying a symlink inside a wrapper |
| Entries must be absolute paths | Relative resolves, against the case directory | Trying a relative one |
| A bare name is looked up as an installed plugin | There is no name lookup at all | Trying three genuinely installed names |
| A `Stop` hook's verdicts cannot be forged | A spawned process writes one after the hook exits | Writing the attack |
| The `deny file-write*` rule was applying | It was not: the profile named `/tmp/...`, the kernel resolves to `/private/tmp/...` | Checking the file was absent, not that no error printed |
| My forged-workspace control was a control | It ran with no case selected and could not go red | Mutating the recogniser and watching the test stay green |
| The eval home's `TMPDIR` follows the operator's shell | **`PATH` is the only variable that reaches the sandbox.** `TMPDIR` and `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` both read `<unset>` inside a run | Printing them from the `SessionStart` hook, after eight runs died inside `git worktree add` |
| A hook can check the environment on the agent's behalf | The hook is *more* privileged, so its check answers a question nobody asked | `/usr/bin/git --version` succeeded in the hook in a run where the agent's Bash could not |
| A suite runs the cases I wrote | Case discovery is a recursive glob and follows symlinked units into *their* eval directories | Two `spec-double-compiler` cases appearing in a run of a different repository's suite |

Read the right-hand column. **Not one of those was found by thinking harder.**

### The six habits, in the order they pay

1. **Probe; do not reason.** A case that fails to load never runs an agent, so a
   refusal costs **$0.00**. Every schema fact in this file came from a
   deliberately malformed case. Reasoning about an undocumented tool produces
   confident prose and nothing else.

2. **Make your failing case fail first.** The attack that proved verdicts were
   forgeable did not work on the first try: an embedded `\n` in a heredoc became
   a real newline and the payload died on a `SyntaxError`. **"No verdict
   appeared" reads exactly like "no hole".** Run the negative case standalone
   and confirm it does the bad thing before you conclude anything prevents it.

3. **Ask what would look identical if you were wrong.** A denied write prints
   nothing. An allowed write also prints nothing. If your evidence is the
   *absence* of an error, you have not measured — check the artefact. This one
   question would have caught three of the nine rows above.

4. **Mutate the thing under test and watch your control go red.** A control that
   has never failed is a claim. Gutting a recogniser and finding the suite still
   green is how the flagship forgery control was exposed as vacuous — it had
   been running with no case selected since the day it was written.

5. **Re-run under the real conditions.** The hook's `HOME` is not your `$HOME`;
   its `python3` is whatever is on `PATH`; its paths resolve physically. A
   verifier that works in your shell and not in the hook withholds verdicts from
   correct work, and the score reads as the agent's failure.

6. **Count the runs behind the number before you quote it.** Fourteen runs of
   one case, while the environment was being repaired monotonically, produced
   Bash-call counts of **14, 10, 9, 8, 18, 18, 15, 27, 19, —, 16, —, 15, 21**.
   The counts did not improve with the environment, never approached the
   budget, and **their spread is wider than every effect that was attributed to
   a change.** Seven single runs were quoted as evidence in that round and all
   seven conclusions were wrong. This is habit 4 pointed at yourself: a number
   you cannot re-produce is a claim.

### The rule for adding to this file

**Before writing a claim here, name the observation that would differ if it were
false.** If you cannot name one, you have a belief, and it goes in marked as a
belief — the way the `agents:` paragraph in §3.5 is marked *I have not run
that*. An unmarked guess in a reference that other skills import is how one
person's ignorance becomes an organisation's.

## 1. The three things a case can observe

This is the whole surface. Six grader types, and they see between them exactly
three things:

| grader | what it reads |
|---|---|
| `file_exists` | **a path in the workspace**, after the run. Globs allowed |
| `tool_used` | **a tool NAME** was called, with a count range |
| `tool_order` | one tool name **before** another |
| `regex` | **the final response text** |
| `llm` | **the final response text**, judged by a model, majority of 3 votes |
| `baseline` | the final response text, against a `baseline_file` |

And here is what nothing observes: **file contents, tool inputs, tool outputs,
exit codes.**

Three probes established the boundaries, and each of them refuted something I
had assumed:

* **The `llm` judge sees the final response and nothing else.** A hook wrote
  `banana` into `SECRET.txt`; the criterion was "score 1 only if SECRET.txt
  contains banana".

  | what the agent did | votes |
  |---|---|
  | never mentioned the file | FAIL FAIL FAIL |
  | **read** the file, did not quote it | FAIL FAIL FAIL |
  | quoted its contents in the reply | PASS PASS PASS |

  Not the workspace. Not tool output. The text it ends with.

* **`tool_used` cannot match a command.** The permission-style pattern parses —
  the failure message renders it back — but for `Bash` it matches nothing. A
  run whose only Bash call was literally `echo hello` scored `Bash` **1x** and
  `Bash(echo:*)` **0x** in the same run. There is no grader that can assert
  *this command ran*.

* **`file_exists` has no content filter.** `contains:` is rejected as an
  unrecognised key; `regex` rejects `path:` and `file:`. A path grader knows
  only that a path exists.

**Consequence, and it is the whole reason for section 3:** with only these,
every claim about *quality* has to be routed through the response — and the
response is written by the thing being graded.

---

## 2. Running one

```bash
HOME=$EVALHOME CLAUDE_CODE_WALNUT_SPIRE=1 \
  claude plugin eval <plugin-dir> \
      --case '<glob>' --ablation none --runs 1 --allow-tools Bash Write Edit
```

Each part is load-bearing, and each was learned from a run that scored 0 for a
reason that was not the agent's.

**`CLAUDE_CODE_WALNUT_SPIRE=1`** — the subcommand is gated behind it and does
not exist without it.

**`--allow-tools`** — the operator grant, and it is **separate from the case's
`allowed_tools:`**. Listing `Write` in the case grants nothing. Running with
`--allow-tools Bash` against a case declaring `[Bash, Write, Edit]` produced

```
not granted (missing --allow-tools grant, or a malformed entry): Write, Edit
```

once, in a per-case note, and a score of 0 — an agent that could read the
program and could not write one line of a spec, reported as a failure to model.
**Assert this in a test**: read `allowed_tools` from the case, read the
documented command from your README, and fail if a gated tool is in the first
and not the second.

**`--ablation none` vs the default** — the default runs a second arm with no
plugin and reports the delta. That is a real control and worth having, but only
if the second arm can do the task. If your fixture is placed by a plugin hook
(section 3), the no-plugin arm gets an **empty workspace** and its 0 means "the
fixture was never placed", not "the skill is what scored". Use `--ablation
none` until the fixture can be placed independently of the plugin.

**`--case <glob>`** — a name filter, and it is **not optional once your units
are symlinked.** Discovery is a recursive glob — `--help` says the cases are
`<eval dir>/**/case.yaml` — so it descends through a symlinked unit into
whatever eval directory *that* unit ships. Verified here: this repository ships
`examples/agent_integration/eval-plugin/evals/` with two cases of its own, and a
suite that symlinks this skill's surface runs them, billed, alongside its own.
The cost is silent — the extra cases score, and nothing says they were not
yours. §3.5 has the shape that makes this bite.

**`--keep-temp`** — preserves each run's sandbox and prints the path. Open it:

```bash
chmod 700 <kept> <kept>/sealed && chmod -R u+rX <kept>/sealed
```

The workspace is `<kept>/sealed/home/cwd`; the full event stream is
`<kept>/out/trace.jsonl`. **Read the trace before you believe a score.** The
trace is where hook exit codes, per-turn tool calls, and `error_max_turns` are
visible, and the summary line shows none of them.

### The home

On a machine with Docker Desktop, a Bash-granting run refuses:

> the Docker (`~/.docker`, `DOCKER_CONFIG`) credential store on this machine
> holds a symbolic link inside it, so the Bash sandbox cannot reliably exclude it

`~/.docker` holds Docker Desktop's CLI shims — 18 symlinks under `bin/` and
`cli-plugins/`, none of them credentials. Two things that do not work:
`DOCKER_CONFIG` pointed at a plain directory (the message is byte-identical, so
the check reads `~/.docker` regardless of the override it names), and a bare
`HOME` override (the sandbox passes and the session cannot authenticate —
`Not logged in - Please run /login` — even with `.claude` and `.claude.json`
symlinked in).

**The credential lives in the keychain, and the keychain path is
HOME-relative.** Symlink `Library/Keychains` and both hold at once:

```bash
EVALHOME=/path/to/scratch/evalhome
mkdir -p "$EVALHOME/.docker" "$EVALHOME/Library"
cp ~/.docker/config.json "$EVALHOME/.docker/config.json"   # the file only
for p in .claude .claude.json .config .cache .local; do
    ln -s "$HOME/$p" "$EVALHOME/$p"
done
ln -s "$HOME/Library/Keychains" "$EVALHOME/Library/Keychains"
```

`.docker` must be a real directory holding a real file; symlinking it to
`~/.docker` puts the shims back.

**What this home does NOT leak — a correction, because I got it wrong once.**
An earlier draft of this section said symlinking `.claude` loads the operator's
personal skills into every run, and named `deep-research`, `dataviz` and
`code-review` as evidence. That was inference, not measurement, and the
measurement says otherwise: a run's `init` event listed **17 skills, every one
of them a Claude Code built-in**, plus the plugin under test. None of the
operator's 20 skill-manager units appeared, even though they are symlinked into
`~/.claude/skills/` and `~/.claude` is symlinked into this home.

The reason is stronger than a config directory. The run gets a **fresh HOME**:
the kept sandbox's `sealed/home/` holds `.aws .config .git .gitconfig .local
cwd` and **no `.claude` at all**, alongside its own per-run config dir with its
own `settings.json`, `projects/` and `sessions/`. `$EVALHOME` is not the run's
`HOME` either — it is what the CLI authenticates from before the sandbox is
built. **The run is more hermetic than I claimed, and your own skills are NOT
there unless you put them there** — which is section 3.5.

Why the wrong inference looked like evidence, since it is the useful part:
`deep-research`, `dataviz` and `code-review` all appear in the **zero-plugin**
arm too. They were built-ins the whole time, and naming three of them as
"the operator's personal skills" was a guess that happened to fit.

### Which copy of your CLI answers — and how to make it the checkout

**By default, it is not your checkout.** The run inherits the operator's whole
interactive `PATH`, `~/.skill-manager/bin/cli` is on it, and a
`which -a tla-spec-dev` inside a run returned

```
/Users/hayde/.skill-manager/bin/cli/tla-spec-dev
/Users/hayde/.skill-manager/bin/cli/tla-spec-dev
/Users/hayde/.skill-manager/bin/cli/tla-spec-dev
```

and nothing else. In another run, 32 of 55 Bash calls touched
`~/.skill-manager` and a traceback resolved the code from
`~/.skill-manager/skills/<unit>/scripts/`. **The plugin's skill directory
loaded correctly and the branch under review was still never executed** — the
skill under test was the plugin's, the toolchain under test was whatever was
installed.

Three ways to fix that do not work. Each was measured, not reasoned about:

| attempt | what happened |
|---|---|
| a plugin `bin/` directory | the docs say it joins the Bash tool's `PATH` while the plugin is enabled. Inside `plugin eval` it never appeared |
| `execution.env: {PATH: ...}` in case.yaml | refused: *"only EVAL_\* keys can be set from case.yaml. Anything else must come from the operator's shell."* |
| a shim under `/tmp` | the shell `PATH` **does** reach the run — it was first in `$PATH` — but the sandbox cannot reach `/private/tmp`, so `which` never found it |

The refusal message names the answer. **Ship a shim inside the checkout and let
the operator prepend it:**

```sh
# <plugin>/bin/<your-cli>
set -eu
here=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)
repo=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$here/../../../.." && pwd)
test -f "$repo/scripts/<entry>.py" || {
    echo "shim: no checkout at $repo -- refusing to fall through to an" \
         "installed copy, which would grade code nobody is reviewing" >&2
    exit 127
}
exec python3 "$repo/scripts/<entry>.py" "$@"
```

```bash
PATH="<plugin>/bin:$PATH" claude plugin eval <plugin-dir> ...
```

Verified: `which -a` then lists the checkout's shim first, ahead of the
installed copies. **The shim refuses rather than falling through** — a shim
that silently defers to the installed CLI reintroduces the exact bug it exists
to fix, and does it invisibly.

Then have the `SessionStart` hook *say which one it got*, and warn when it is
not the shim, so the trace answers the question without anyone having to
reconstruct it:

```
  tla-spec-dev: <plugin>/bin/tla-spec-dev  (THE CHECKOUT under review)
```

### Dependent tools

A skill declares `cli_dependencies` and then assumes they are there. The eval
sandbox is not your shell: have the `SessionStart` hook resolve each one and
print it, missing ones included.

```
  java:      /usr/bin/java
  tla2tools: ~/.skill-manager/bin/cli/.spec-double-compiler/tla2tools.jar
  pytest:    /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.10/bin/pytest
  jinja2:    NOT ON PATH
```

`NOT ON PATH` printed before turn one is a truthful input. The same fact
discovered on turn 30 is a turn-ceiling failure that reads as an agent who
could not do the work.

---

## 3. Adding a skill, and placing a fixture

### The plugin

A directory with `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`:

```json
{"name": "<name>-eval", "version": "0.1.0", "experimental": {"evals": "evals"}}
```

and the skill surface under `skills/<skill-name>/`. **Symlink it, do not copy
it** — a copy drifts from the repository it claims to test. Verified loaded: a
passing run's `init` event listed the plugin, and the agent invoked
`Skill(<plugin>:<skill>)`.

One plugin holds **many cases** — `evals/<case-name>/` per case. You do not
need a plugin per case.

**But hooks belong to the plugin, not to a case**, so one `SessionStart` hook
has to serve every case. `execution.env` is the channel, and the allowlist that
refuses `PATH` is exactly what it is for:

```yaml
execution:
  env:
    EVAL_CASE: catch-the-drift
```

```sh
case "${EVAL_CASE:-}" in
  scaffold-a-program-model) ... ;;
  catch-the-drift)          ... ;;
  "")  echo "EVAL_CASE unset" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
```

Verified: a case setting `EVAL_CASE` had it visible in the hook. **Fail loudly
when it is unset** — a hook that silently places nothing is the empty-repository
failure again, and it reads as an agent who could not work.

Keep the shared scripts **outside** `evals/` (`<plugin>/lib/`). A directory
under `evals/` with no `case.yaml` is not loaded as a case today, but putting
library code where the loader is scanning invites a name to become meaningful
later.

If `plugin eval` refuses your repository with *"a plugin directory holds more
than 20000 entries"*, that is what the thin symlinked plugin is for: carry the
skill's surface and nothing else.

### `scaffold_script:` does not run — use a hook

A case may declare `scaffold_script:` and the CLI has a `--scaffold` flag that
prints a warning about running it. **The script is never executed.** Measured at
every placement — top level, `execution:`, `setup:`, `workspace:`, `sandbox:`,
`scaffold.script` — and in both forms, a file name and inline bash. The
decisive probe was an inline body of `echo ... >&2; exit 3`: the case still
scored 1.00, so it was not failing quietly, it was never invoked.

Place fixtures from a **`SessionStart` hook** in `hooks/hooks.json`. One hook
serves every case and dispatches on `EVAL_CASE` (see above), so it lives beside
the plugin rather than inside a case:

```json
{"hooks": {"SessionStart": [{"hooks": [
  {"type": "command", "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/lib/place.sh"}
]}]}}
```

**Fail with exit 2, not exit 1.** Claude Code treats 2 as blocking and every
other non-zero code as advisory, so a placement hook that exits 1 prints its
complaint and lets the session start anyway — on a workspace it just failed to
set up. Where a case seeds a deliberate fault, that is the difference between
refusing and handing the agent a program with nothing wrong with it, which
scores well for doing nothing.

It runs with the workspace as its working directory, before the first turn, and
the trace records `hook_response … exit_code 0`. Locate the fixture from `$0`,
never from the working directory and never from a guessed environment variable:
a `${EVAL_CASE_DIR:-.}` whose `.` fallback resolved to the workspace copied
nothing, and the case scored 0 on an empty repository. What that reads as is
"the agent could not build a spec". What it meant was "there was nothing to
build one from".

### Hand the session its toolchain

A case that makes the agent find its own tools measures the search, not the
skill. One run spent **39 of its 40 turns** on `find / -maxdepth 8 -iname
"tla2tools*.jar"`, a scan of `/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines` and an `unzip`
of the jar, hit the turn ceiling, and left behind a scratch module about a
counter mod 3.

Have the `SessionStart` hook discover the tools **at runtime** and print what it
found. Nothing hardcoded: another machine gets its own paths, or gets told the
tool is missing, which is a truthful input rather than a silent 0.

### Five environment facts, each of which cost a failed run

From the `skill-manager` suite. Each was paid for once; a suite that does not
know them pays again, and every one of them bills as a skill failure.

1. **`PATH` is the only variable that reaches the sandbox.** `TMPDIR` and
   `SKILL_MANAGER_HOME` both printed `<unset>` from inside a run, even though
   both were set in the operator's shell. `execution.env` will not close the
   gap either — its allowlist refuses everything but `EVAL_*`:

   > `execution.env` key PATH is not allowed — only `EVAL_*` keys can be set
   > from case.yaml. Anything else must come from the operator's shell.

   Read those two sentences together: `PATH` has to come from the shell, and
   `PATH` is the only part of the shell that arrives — `TMPDIR` was set there
   too and did not. **Anything your case needs that is not a `PATH` entry or an
   `EVAL_*` key has to be discovered inside the run.**

2. **An unset `TMPDIR` breaks Apple's `git` before it does anything.** `git`
   from the Xcode command-line tools writes an `xcrun` cache into `TMPDIR` on
   startup. Without one:

   ```
   git: error: couldn't create cache file '…/T/xcrun_db-…' (Operation not permitted)
   ```

   and `git worktree add` dies immediately after printing *"Preparing
   worktree"*. **One unset variable made a case unmeasurable for eight runs** —
   eight reds on a case whose task began with a worktree command, not one of
   them about the skill under test.

3. **The sandbox cannot read under the operator's home directory.** The same
   command succeeded in an ordinary shell and failed inside a run. Build trees,
   fixtures and checkouts have to live where the sandbox reaches — `/private/tmp`
   worked, which is where it keeps its own temps.

   > **This does not agree with the `/private/tmp` row in §2**, which says a
   > shim there was on `PATH` and `which` never found it. The two observations
   > are not the same observation — one is *resolving an executable on `PATH`*,
   > the other is *reading a tree* — and they are from different suites on
   > different machines, one of them a CLI patch apart. **Which of read access,
   > exec access and `PATH` resolution `/private/tmp` actually gets is
   > UNDECIDED**, and the row stays until somebody runs the probe that
   > separates them: put a readable file and an executable shim in one
   > `/private/tmp` directory and have the hook print `cat` and `which` for
   > each. That probe costs one refused case, i.e. $0.00.

4. **A CLI shim may exec a toolchain of its own.** The checkout shim in §2 ends
   in `exec`, and what it execs has its own dependencies — theirs runs `jbang`.
   Putting the shim's directory on the eval `PATH` is not enough; **everything
   the shim reaches for has to be on that `PATH` too**, and the `SessionStart`
   hook should print each of them the way §"Dependent tools" prints the rest.

5. **A hook cannot verify the environment on the agent's behalf.** Measured: the
   `SessionStart` hook ran `/usr/bin/git --version` successfully in a run where
   the agent's own Bash could not. The hook is outside the sandbox — that is the
   same asymmetry §4 relies on to run TLC, read in the opposite direction, and
   it is worse here because it is *silent*. A hook that checks a tool and prints
   `OK` has confirmed the tool works **for the hook**, and the run proceeds into
   an environment nobody has actually tested.

### Prove the environment in setup, before a run is billed against it

The consequence of all five, and it is the cheapest rule in this file.

**Setup must run the real front-door command and fail if it does not work.**
Not a version probe, not a `which` — the actual first command the case will ask
the agent for, in a throwaway corner of the fixture, from the same place the
agent will stand:

```sh
verify_env() {                     # last thing setup.sh does
    tmp=$(mktemp -d)
    ( cd "$tmp" && <the real front-door command> ) >"$tmp/log" 2>&1 || {
        echo "setup: environment cannot run the task — refusing to bill a run" >&2
        cat "$tmp/log" >&2
        exit 1
    }
    rm -rf "$tmp"
}
```

It costs **$0.00** — a case that never starts runs no agent — and in that suite
it caught three broken environments that would otherwise have been billed, and
reported, as skill failures. Facts 2 and 3 above are both things `verify_env`
would have caught on run one instead of run eight.

**This is not the `.eval/toolchain` marker of §4, and it does not replace it.**
The marker annotates a run that happened; `verify_env` stops the run from
happening. You want both: the marker cannot rescue a score (§4 is explicit that
`file_exists` has no UNDECIDED), and setup refusing is the only mechanism that
keeps the unmeasurable run out of the report entirely.
